About us

The Audit Office aims to improve trust and confidence in the public sector. Under the mandate of the Controller and Auditor-General, the Office completes statutory audits of all public organisations (around 3300 annually) and carries out performance audits, inquiries, and other auditing and assurance services. Through this work, the Office provides Parliament and the public an independent view of how public organisations are operating and providing value for money. In early 2026, we finalised some changes to set us up to achieve our ambition and carry out our work programme, and to become a more modern, high-performing organisation. Our new name - The Audit Office | Te Mana Arotake - is part of this work, unifying the Office of the Auditor-General and Audit New Zealand. While The Audit Office becomes our outward-facing name, our official name, established under the Public Audit Act 2001, remains The Controller and Auditor-General.

    We have written to the Minister of Housing, Hon Chris Bishop, and the Cabinet Office about how the Minister’s constituency interests were managed in decisions to fund the City Link bridge in Lower Hutt. When Ministers make decisions that might affect their own electorates, the public needs to be able to see that any constituency interests have been carefully identified and managed. We found that the relevant constituency interest had been identified and that an agreed management plan was in place. We did not see evidence that the Minister’s constituency interest was behind the decision to approve the funding variation. However, we considered more could have been done to manage the perception risks involved. Read the full letter on our website: https://lnkd.in/enwfeKvv

    Today, we published our inquiry report into the Healthy School Lunches Programme. This looked at how the Ministry of Education developed options, procured suppliers, put the contract in place, and monitored performance. The new model for the programme has saved money in 2025, but our report found that the Ministry is not able to clearly show whether the programme is delivering the outcomes it set out to achieve. 1. To demonstrate value for money, the Ministry needs to show that the programme is achieving its intended outcomes, not just that it has reduced costs. 2. Late changes to the scope and price of the procurement raised fairness concerns for suppliers. 3. The Ministry’s back-up planning was inadequate for a programme of this size and risk, and supplier problems materialised early in the rollout. 4. The programme has delivered savings, but the Ministry needs to focus on ongoing performance issues, such as nutrition, waste, and surplus. We encourage the Ministry to consider how it measures and reports the overall value for money of the school lunches programme. The Ministry has told us that it has recently made improvements to its procurement and contract management practices for 2026 and beyond. Watch our short video and read the full report: https://lnkd.in/ejw9XzgG

    Loved having Trevor with us for the past nine weeks as our Auckland University of Technology intern. All the best for your next chapter, and maybe we'll see you back here again!

    Trevor Coetzee
    3w

    Wrapping up my 9-week internship The Audit Office, New Zealand Grateful for an experience that challenged me, made me step outside my comfort zone, built my confidence, moved me to a new city, and gave me real insight into the public sector. A standout highlight for me was writing and presenting a briefing to a Select Committee, an experience that pushed me to communicate clearly, think critically, and deliver under pressure. Over the 9 weeks, I developed my skills in: - critical thinking - professional writing - translating complex information into clear insights I also had the chance to explore how AI might be used in audit, which really challenged how I think about risk, accountability, and the future of work. As a Pasifika student, being part of a supportive environment and network made this experience even more meaningful. Representation and community matter. Huge thank you to everyone who supported me along the way, I’ve learned a lot and I’m excited for what’s next.

    Stable housing is an important part of helping people successfully return to the community after leaving prison. This week, we appeared before Parliament’s Justice Committee to discuss our report, “Department of Corrections: Planning for stable housing outcomes”. The Committee was interested in several issues covered in the report, including support for people on remand (people in custody waiting to be tried or sentenced), what is known about people’s housing needs when they leave prison, and how well Corrections understands the effectiveness of its housing support work. The Committee also heard from Corrections, which agreed that stable housing is important to successful reintegration and to reduce re-offending. It accepts our recommendations and is working to implement them. Watch the Justice Committee appearance here 📽️ https://lnkd.in/dxE-3T5n (We’ve added a comment with approximate timestamps if you’d like to jump to a particular topic) Read our report 👉 https://lnkd.in/dEPr2rPc

    Happy Scrutiny Week! Over the next few days, select committees will be examining the Estimates of Appropriations - that is, the Government’s spending plans for the year ahead. The Audit Office plays an important role in the scrutiny process. We’ve prepared nearly 70 briefing papers to highlight what we see as the key areas for committees to consider. Our sector managers and advisors, alongside our auditors, will also be briefing committees in person throughout the week before the ministers come in for the public sessions. The Scrutiny Week schedule is available at https://lnkd.in/dJfDP7zx, and you can also watch any of the public Estimates hearings online. Photographed is Lyndsey Gibson, Sector Manager, and Chrissie Murray, Audit Director, at the Justice Committee today.
